facts.text: Families keep folded road atlases in the glove compartment for trips beyond familiar roads.
Drivers print directions from a computer before leaving for an unfamiliar address.
Some drivers use dashboard navigation units that give spoken turn instructions.
Most drivers still ask for directions or consult road signs when lost.
Parents buckle young children into car seats or booster seats before driving.
A family loads luggage into a minivan for a summer road trip.
Pickup trucks carry tools and supplies between farms, homes, and local shops.
Some families choose sport utility vehicles for passenger room and cargo space.
Teenagers study the driver's manual before taking a written permit test.
A new driver practices parking and turning with a parent in the passenger seat.
Students wait beside neighborhood roads for the morning school bus.
A school bus driver checks mirrors before pulling away from a stop.
Children ride bicycles to friends' houses where local roads allow it.
A cyclist wears a helmet while riding along a neighborhood street.
Families stop at highway rest areas to stretch and use the restroom.
Travelers check highway exit signs for fuel, food, and lodging.
Drivers pay highway tolls with cash or an electronic toll pass where available.
A gas station customer usually pumps fuel without an attendant.
Drivers can pay for gasoline with a card at many fuel pumps.
Rising gasoline costs prompt some commuters to combine errands into one trip.
Hybrid passenger cars become more visible on American roads during the decade.
A mechanic connects diagnostic equipment to a car to investigate an engine warning light.
A driver calls roadside assistance after a flat tire or breakdown.
Intercity buses connect some small towns with larger cities through scheduled stops.
Passenger trains serve selected routes, but many small towns have no train stop.
Some commuters arrange shared rides to work to save fuel and parking costs.
